items.text: Matter A-1: Hartwell v. Telltale Cardiac Systems, Ashgrove County Superior Court, Case No. 25-CV-03817. The client, defendant Telltale Cardiac Systems, is represented by Kenge, Carboy & Vholes LLP (partner Walter Osgood, associate Priya Raghunathan). Plaintiff Dorothea Hartwell filed her complaint on March 4, 2025, with Farrar Whitlock (Gideon Farrar) as plaintiff's counsel.

Plaintiff alleges the conductor coil of the ArcLine AL-4120 bipolar active-fixation pacing lead was unreasonably prone to fatigue fracture, that a safer alternative design was feasible, that Telltale knew of a heightened fracture rate before her implant, and that Telltale failed to warn implanting physicians of fracture risk near the clavicle and first rib. She also seeks punitive damages.

The AL-4120 was implanted in Ms. Hartwell on or about March 19, 2019, at Westmarch Regional Hospital, via a subclavian approach. A routine interrogation on November 8, 2022 showed out-of-range impedance, and a lead revision surgery was performed on November 15, 2022. Radiographs show the break about 4 cm from the pectoral pocket, where the lead crosses beneath the clavicle.

Damages claimed or estimated: plaintiff demands compensatory damages above $1,900,000 plus punitive damages. Medical expenses are about $214,000 (revision surgery, billed charges). Lost earnings as a school administrator are roughly $96,000. The associate's October 7, 2025 memo estimates realistic verdict exposure of $450,000 to $900,000 if liability is found.

Telltale's complaint database shows 31 confirmed conductor fractures out of about 22,000 AL-4120 leads shipped, a rate near 0.14 percent. The firm still needs engineering to confirm that the rate stayed within the labeled range, because plaintiff will use a 2021 trend report to argue notice of a rising fracture rate.

A 2020 internal note from a field engineer observed that returned leads showed wear from repeated bending near the pocket and suggested the design be revisited. It has not been produced. The associate regards it as the most damaging undisclosed document.

Telltale ran an internal quality inquiry in 2021 into returned-lead fractures (the 'Larkspur review'), which preceded the 2021 trend report. As of the October 7, 2025 memo, plaintiff had not asked about it by name.

The AL-4120 instructions for use warn against medial subclavian puncture and describe lateral venous access as the preferred approach. The operative note does not say which technique was used. The memo calls this the most important open factual question.

Filing status of the answer: the April 22, 2025 Answer and Affirmative Defenses was a draft for partner review, not yet filed. It denies defect, inadequate warnings and causation. It pleads fifteen defenses, including learned intermediary, adequate warnings, state of the art, regulatory compliance and preemption, no feasible safer alternative, causation, superseding cause, comparative fault, mitigation, limitations and repose, misuse, setoff, and punitive damages.

Open drafting notes on the draft answer: (a) whether to plead repose given the 2019 implant date; (b) client sign-off is needed on the preemption language; (c) the Eleventh Defense (limitations and repose) is a placeholder pending plaintiff's chart.

Telltale's pleaded position is that the AL-4120 was not defectively designed and its labeling was adequate. It says its duty to warn ran to the implanting physician, who exercised independent medical judgment. It also says any fracture resulted from implant technique, lead positioning, patient anatomy or activity, or the acts of third parties.
The firm's position (October 2025 memo) is that the statute of repose is likely unavailable given the 2019 implant date, and it recommends dropping the repose defense from the final answer.

Plaintiff served her First Set of Requests for Production in June 2025. They sought AL-4120 design history files from concept through the 2018 release, complaint and returned-product analyses for any ArcLine lead from 2015 to the present, and all fatigue and flex testing of the conductor coil.

Telltale's discovery position is that production should be limited to the AL-4120, not the whole ArcLine family. It argues that models differ in conductor coil pitch and insulation thickness, so family-wide requests are disproportionate. Plaintiff's counsel counters that Telltale's labeling treats ArcLine as a single platform. He said he would consider limiting the request to the AL-4120 and its closest sibling if given an engineering declaration on the coil differences.

Agreed on June 18, 2025: complaint and returned-product records for the AL-4120 will run from its 2018 clinical-use start to the November 15, 2022 revision date. Telltale refused to produce post-revision events for leads returned from the implanting center, calling them beyond its knowledge of its own product and third-party patient information. Plaintiff's counsel had asked for them, and Telltale invited a motion if he intended to pursue it.

Telltale offered an informal engineering declaration limited to coil differences between the AL-4120 and the AL-4125, on the express condition that it is not a concession of family-wide relevance. The firm's strategy is for that declaration to hold the line on those two models against further pressure for sibling-model files.

Expert schedule agreed by email June 19, 2025, subject to court approval of a stipulation: plaintiff's opening expert reports are due January 16, 2026, and Telltale's reports are due March 17, 2026. Both sides agreed that drafts and attorney-expert communications are protected, except for facts, data and assumptions counsel provided, and that consulting experts are not discoverable.

Plaintiff expects to call a biomedical engineer (Dr. Ruth Kellaway) on stress concentration from coil pitch and insulation sleeve, an electrophysiologist (Dr. Leopold Quist) on causation of symptoms and revision, and a regulatory witness who will say warnings should have been updated after a 2021 trend report. Telltale's testifying design engineer is Dr. Henrik Vandermeer.
As of the October 2025 memo, Dr. Kellaway had not examined the explanted lead under magnification and had not ruled out subclavian crush from medial puncture.

The firm's strategy is to direct its first motion practice and first expert effort at the reliability and fit of Dr. Quist's and Dr. Kellaway's causation opinions, not the design-defect debate. If their opinion that the lead failed from design rather than placement is limited, the design theory loses its link to the injury. Only if that motion fails would the firm meet the design theory directly through Dr. Vandermeer.

The firm recommends starting the industry-standards defense now rather than waiting for Dr. Kellaway's reports. It would retain a separate witness from the cardiac-device standards community, distinct from Dr. Vandermeer, to avoid a 'grading his own work' attack and to keep Vandermeer out of standards-committee questions.

The treating cardiologist, Dr. Anselm Teague, is the only witness who can say whether lateral or medial access was used and what he understood from the instructions for use. His deposition was first proposed for the week of September 15, 2025, then slipped and was reset to November 6, 2025. Telltale had proposed that expert depositions follow all fact depositions including his. Plaintiff refused to defer them all until after him.

Risk outcome of the open operative-technique question: if Dr. Teague used medial puncture, Telltale's defense gets stronger. If he used the lateral approach, plaintiff's inherent-fatigue-weakness theory gains weight.

Client instruction: Telltale will make no settlement offer until the treating cardiologist has been deposed and the transcript read. Counsel must not engage on figures or signal willingness to pay before then. Afterward, counsel sends an assessment and recommended range to General Counsel Marguerite Salvesen for the claims committee. Authority above $500,000 needs sign-off from CFO Cormac Brightwater.

Settlement posture: the firm has told plaintiff's counsel only that it cannot discuss numbers. Plaintiff's counsel has asked twice for a mediation date. The firm recommends declining until after the November 6, 2025 deposition and, if the transcript is favorable, proposing mediation in January 2026, with an authority request only after the deposition.

Client requirement on experts: Telltale must be consulted before any testifying expert is engaged (three names per discipline with prior testimony notes). Its regulatory affairs group, led by Odalys Fennimore, must review every expert report before service, to check consistency with what Telltale told the regulator. The group needs ten business days, and reports may not be shared outside the firm and the experts until cleared.

The firm proposes that Dr. Vandermeer deliver a near-final draft by January 30, 2026 so the regulatory review does not compress editing before the March 17, 2026 deadline. Regulatory group comments should go through counsel and be logged so the exchange stays protected as work done at counsel's direction. The firm will confirm with plaintiff's counsel that the drafts stipulation covers this process.

Client reporting and handling requirements: a monthly written update and a call after significant events. An initial case assessment was due within 45 days of the March 27, 2025 letter. Five business days' notice is required before any motion. Phase budgets are required with variance explained over ten percent. All communications go to Ms. Salvesen with a copy to insurance liaison Thaddeus Wren. Priya Raghunathan is the day-to-day contact, with a call every two weeks early on.

Client guidelines: no contact with media, treating physicians, or Telltale employees below vice president level without clearing it with the General Counsel. Preserve all AL-4120 and ArcLine documents (a litigation hold was issued). No more than two timekeepers at a deposition are paid for. Invoices are monthly in task-based format. Design engineering and complaint-handling records are confidential, and a protective order should be proposed before producing anything.

Client wants a vigorous but measured defense and asked the firm to avoid public filings that characterize failure rates further than the case requires, because Telltale is in a regulatory inspection tied to its next-generation lead. Telltale says the AL-4120 has a long field record supported by its own complaint data, and that it believes the lead was not defective.

Budget: the client's working assumption is that the case should be resolved or tried for under $500,000 in fees and costs combined, and it wants an explanation if the firm expects more. The firm's estimate through trial is $410,000 to $520,000. Telltale's product liability program has a $750,000 self-insured retention per claim, and coverage matters go only to Mr. Wren or Ms. Salvesen.

Complaint data is tracked in Orrinwick, Telltale's complaint-handling database. The client offered interviews in April 2025 with its director of reliability engineering, the quality engineer who did the device history review, and the clinical specialist covering the implanting hospital.

Other identified risks: Ms. Hartwell is a credible witness who has had a hard recovery (sympathy risk), and plaintiff's counsel is expected to keep pressing for sibling-model files (discovery creep). Next steps in the memo: finalize the Teague deposition outline, get Dr. Vandermeer's CV and availability, outline a motion to exclude Drs. Quist and Kellaway, and send Ms. Salvesen the November status note.
